C0.quote: designer collects participants’ type reports and chooses an allocation through some publicly announced mechanism
C0.note: The paper studies allocation mechanisms and also voting in Appendix A.3.

C1.quote: We provide a tight characterization of maximally auditable DA-representable mechanisms (Theorem 1).
C1.note: The paper's main results are axiomatic characterizations of mechanisms by auditability properties.

C2.1.quote: Each individual i has a type report θi ∈ Θi

C2.2.quote: an individual’s type report is represented by a pair of a preference ranking and a vector of priority scores

C2.3.quote: Each individual i ∈ I has a strict preference ranking Pi over objects O

C2.4.quote: An allocation is a bijection ω : I → O
C2.4.note: The paper studies allocation mechanisms where agents report types; the relation between reported types and held attitudes is not discussed explicitly. The input is treated as the held type report.

C3.1.quote: participants do not fully observe each others’ type reports
C3.1.note: The paper studies auditability, which is not about strategic voters. Voters are not modeled as strategic in the analyses.

C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their held attitudes.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost, distortion, or intensity of preference notions used for voters.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: we say a mechanism ϕ weakly Pareto dominates a mechanism ψ

C5.2.quote: if for any problem θ = (P, r), and any i ∈ I, either ϕc (θ)(i)Pi ψ(θ)(i) or ϕc (θ)(i) = ψ(θ)(i)
C5.2.note: Evaluation uses the reported preferences as the basis for Pareto domination, with no statement relating them to held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: participants do not fully observe each others’ type reports
VOT.quote_info: participants know and observe their own type reports and outcomes, but not necessarily those of others
VOT.note: Voters do not take strategic actions in the model; their type reports are given.

ORG.note: No organiser takes actions in the model.

DIS.note: No district designer in the formal model.

DES.note: No mechanism designer modeled with choices or objectives.

C7.1.quote: participants do not fully observe each others’ type reports

C8.1.note: No strategic or mixed types present.

C9.1.quote: our findings may contribute to discussions on choosing a mechanism for real-life problems

claims.quote: our findings may contribute to discussions on choosing a mechanism for real-life problems
Our findings potentially highlight the importance of addressing trust and transparency considerations for real-life assignment problems.
the need for transparency and auditability in school choice has been highlighted

C9.1.note: The paper makes real-world claims about school choice and other allocation mechanisms.

C9.2.quote: our findings may contribute to discussions on choosing a mechanism for real-life problems
C9.2.note: Needed assumption not stated: that the type reports and outcomes observable in the model correspond to what participants can observe in real settings.

C10.1.note: No explicit statement that the paper studies the rule only as a function of submitted inputs, nor that it takes no position on the relation between inputs and held attitudes.
